An employee option grant is not a cash balance: chart vesting, exercise cost and the price spread

Four interactive charts separate an authored vesting schedule, vested intrinsic spread, an assumed exercise-and-sale reconciliation and the cash needed to exercise and hold.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a fixed, authored 48-month option schedule with a 12-month cliff

Interactive planning lab

Vested option units under the authored schedule450
Intrinsic spread on vested units, before tax and fees · CAD$4,500
Exercise-and-hold strike-cash shortfall, before tax and fees · CAD$17,500

Original CAD illustration, not an actual employee award, option valuation, tax estimate or recommendation to exercise. Each option unit buys one share at the entered strike price. The fixed authored schedule vests nothing through month 11, catches up completed service at month 12, then vests cumulatively each completed month through month 48. Cumulative units are rounded down to whole units; all remaining units vest at month 48. Continued service and an open exercise window are assumed at the chosen checkpoint; no expiry date, forfeiture, prior exercise, rolling grant, performance condition or blackout is modeled. All units remain unexercised when the snapshot is taken. Intrinsic spread is vested units times max(share price minus strike, zero); it is not full option fair value, owned stock or money already received. The exercise-and-sale waterfall assumes a permitted immediate sale at the same selected price, with no change between exercise and sale. It shows zero transaction flows at or below strike, a plotting convention rather than an exercise policy. The separate cash comparison concerns exercise and hold, which receives shares rather than sale cash. Uncommitted cash is not spent in the model. Taxes, withholding, fees, trading restrictions, settlement, borrowing and subsequent price changes are excluded; actual terms and cash requirements can differ.

The central idea

Read the grant’s terms before assigning dollars to a goal. Vested units, owned shares, intrinsic spread and spendable sale proceeds are different quantities.

01

A right to buy shares is different from owning shares or receiving cash

A compensation statement may display a large option count without showing money that can pay next month’s rent. The count needs a contract, a time condition and an exercise price before it can become a useful planning input.

Investor.gov distinguishes employee stock options from an employee stock ownership retirement plan. An option gives a right to buy company shares at a specified price after the relevant conditions. The grant itself does not mean the employee already owns all the underlying shares.

This article uses a fictional grant in Canadian dollars. It is a cash-arithmetic illustration rather than a description of a particular Canadian or U.S. award. Each authored unit buys one share. Keep the granted count, vested count, strike payment, share-sale proceeds and actual cash received on separate lines of the plan.

02

The cliff controls when service first produces vested units

The default grant contains 1,200 units. The authored schedule lasts 48 months, with nothing vested through month eleven. At month twelve, it catches up the completed service and vests 300 units. Another 25 units vest per completed month under this particular grant size.

At the selected month eighteen, 450 units have vested and 750 remain unvested. The milestone bars are snapshots of that same untouched grant. Adding the bars together would count the grant repeatedly; they are not new awards received each month.

For grant sizes that do not divide evenly, cumulative grant multiplied by completed months divided by 48 is rounded down to whole units. At month 48, every remaining unit vests. The control selects completed service, not a forecast of future employment. This fixed convention is invented for the chart. A real grant agreement may use a different cliff, schedule, performance condition or treatment when employment ends.

03

Multiply vested units by the positive price–strike difference

The default share-price assumption is CAD 60 and the strike is CAD 50. The price difference is CAD 10 per unit, giving 450 × CAD 10 = CAD 4,500 of vested intrinsic spread. Multiplying all 1,200 granted units by CAD 60 would instead describe a hypothetical underlying share amount, not cash owned through the vested options.

Fidelity’s stock-option explanation describes the distinction between the grant’s purchase right and the shares acquired through exercise. Its examples also distinguish vesting from exercise. The chart keeps those steps separate.

The price curve is a sensitivity, not a projected stock path. It floors intrinsic spread at zero when the share price does not exceed strike. That does not value every feature of an unexpired option. The opportunity to exercise later, uncertain future prices and contractual restrictions are outside this calculation. Intrinsic spread is therefore neither full option fair value nor a bank deposit.

04

Deduct the strike from a permitted sale before treating proceeds as a resource

Suppose the 450 vested units can be exercised and the acquired shares sold immediately at CAD 60 each. Gross sale proceeds would be CAD 27,000. Buying those shares at the CAD 50 strike requires CAD 22,500, leaving CAD 4,500 before taxes and transaction costs.

The waterfall reconciles those amounts without adding the spread to the sale proceeds again. The spread is already the difference between the two components. Their chart order is not an instruction about execution or settlement, and the assumed sale is not money already available.

Fidelity’s global stock-plan glossary distinguishes exercise and sell from exercise and hold. A permitted sale-funded arrangement can use proceeds to meet exercise costs and other deductions. This model assumes the first arrangement exists for its waterfall only. At or below strike it shows no transaction, which is a plotting convention rather than an exercise recommendation.

05

Positive intrinsic spread does not supply the cash needed to retain shares

Exercise and hold is a separate comparison. The employee pays the strike and keeps the acquired shares, so this alternative has no share-sale receipt. The default strike payment is still CAD 22,500, even though the calculated intrinsic spread is only CAD 4,500.

With CAD 5,000 of entered uncommitted cash, the strike-only funding gap is CAD 17,500. Comparing the CAD 4,500 spread with the cash balance would miss the larger purchase payment. The cash bars show both amounts and the remaining shortfall without adding them into a fictitious total.

For a separate funded example, suppose those 450 shares are retained after paying the strike, then fall to CAD 40 each. Their value becomes CAD 18,000, below the CAD 22,500 purchase payment. This extra arithmetic is outside the chart’s unchanged-price comparison. Exercising changes an option into a shareholding; a previously positive intrinsic spread does not fix the later sale result.

The input should represent cash free of other commitments. Money reserved for annual bills, an emergency or another goal cannot simultaneously fund the exercise. A zero gap covers only the modeled strike payment; it does not estimate taxes, withholding or fees. The illustration neither borrows the difference nor executes an exercise, and it does not compare the merits of retaining or selling the shares.

06

Use actual award terms and receipt dates before attaching options to a goal

A practical record should identify the award, vested units, strike, exercise window and permitted transaction methods. Keep an expiry date separate from a vesting date. The charts assume the window is open at the selected checkpoint; they do not calculate a deadline or a post-employment exercise period.

Review the real agreement and administrator’s current instructions for restrictions and timing. The cited sources explain general concepts and administration methods, rather than establishing any reader’s contract. Their U.S. tax discussions are not imported into this CAD illustration. No personal tax liability or withholding rate is calculated.

Finally, place only confirmed cash receipts in a dated spending plan. An option grant, a hypothetical quote and an assumed sale are earlier stages. The related employer-share guide examines the additional risk of salary and investment exposure depending on the same company. This page addresses the prior question: what is owned, what must be paid, and what event would actually produce spendable cash?

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts are original hypothetical CAD calculations. The 48-month schedule and 12-month cliff are authored assumptions, and no employer’s award, future price, full option value or tax result is estimated. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Investor.gov · Employee Stock Option Plans ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Primary investor-education source distinguishing an option’s right to buy company stock from an employee stock ownership retirement plan. This article does not model an ESOP or assume a universal grant contract.

  2. Fidelity · What are stock options and how do they work? ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Stock-plan provider’s explanation of the purchase right, strike price, vesting and exercise. The charts use an independently authored schedule and figures; the source’s tax examples and typical terms are not adopted.

  3. Fidelity · Stock Plan Services Global Glossary ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Provider definitions distinguish grant agreement, vesting, exercise and hold, and sale-funded exercise. Actual permissions, deadlines, deductions and availability depend on the specific plan. No transaction is initiated by these charts.
